scenes.headline: How a laptop drives a desktop GPU over one cable
scenes.sub: An Arc Pro B60 on an M1 Max, under Linux
scenes.say: Hi, I'm Fid! Here's how a Mac laptop running Linux drives an Intel card through one Thunderbolt cable.

scenes.text: The weights never cross the cable. What slowed decode was the driver's own small buffers sitting on the laptop's side of it.
scenes.say: The model never crosses the cable. What slowed it was the driver's own small buffers, left on the laptop's side.

steps.say: The laptop runs Linux with sixteen kilobyte pages. Its port carries PCI Express inside a tunnel.
The tunnel ends in a powered box, with the card in a normal slot.
On top, llama dot c p p talks to Intel's Vulkan driver, which sends the card its work.
Every layer of the model sits in the card's own memory.

left.title: Mainline xe
items: Uses the host page as the GPU page
left.say: Intel's kernel driver assumes host pages and GPU pages are the same size.

right.title: The 16K patches
right.say: The patches keep GPU units at four kilobytes, and round host buffers to sixteen.

scenes.title: What the GPU reads on every dispatch

steps.say: The weights and cache were in card memory from the start.
But the CPU writes shader code, descriptors and state, so they landed on the laptop's side.
Every small dispatch fetched them across the cable. Moving them took a small model from about nineteen to sixty six tokens a second.

scenes.text: Over a tunnel, bulk bandwidth is fine. Small reads the driver thinks are local are what cost.
